opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing missing is that these models don't really learn on the job. Today, the way it works is we pour an enormous amount of effort into training, we freeze the weights, and then we ship it. From that point on, the model is essentially static. It can pick things up within a conversation, in context, but the moment that session ends, it's gone. It doesn't carry that forward.

Compare that to a person you hire. On day one they're smart and capable, but they don't know your company, your customers, your internal jargon, the way your systems are wired together. Over weeks and months they get dramatically better because they're absorbing feedback, making mistakes, getting corrected, and internalizing all of that. A model today is perpetually on its first day. You can stuff a bunch of context into the prompt, you can do retrieval, you can fine-tune it periodically, but those are all sort of workarounds. They're not the model genuinely accumulating experience.

So what I'd like to see is models that can take feedback from the people using them, whether that's an explicit correction or just the signal that something worked or didn't, and actually update in a durable way. And do it efficiently, from a handful of examples rather than needing a giant curated dataset and a training run.

There are real hard problems there. You have to avoid catastrophic forgetting, so learning something new doesn't degrade what the model already knows. You need it to be robust, because not all feedback is good feedback, and you don't want a model that can be easily steered into bad behavior by a few bad interactions. And especially for enterprises, there's the question of privacy and isolation: what one customer teaches the model should stay with that customer.

But I think that's the frontier. Raw capability has been climbing fast, and the gap now is less about how smart the model is out of the box and more about whether it can adapt to the specific environment it's deployed in. Whoever cracks continual learning in a practical way is going to unlock a huge amount of value, because suddenly these systems compound. They get better the more you use them, the way a great colleague does.

r001.rationale: The response says models are trained, their weights are frozen, and they remain essentially static after deployment, preventing them from carrying conversational experience forward.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the biggest gap is that today's models are basically frozen at the end of training. You do pretraining, you do post-training, you ship it, and from that moment on the weights are static. Every interaction starts from zero. The model can be brilliant in a single conversation, it can reason its way through something really hard, and then the session ends and all of that is gone. The next time it sees a similar problem it's solving it fresh again.

Humans obviously don't work that way. If I spend a week struggling with something and finally figure it out, I'm a different person at the end of that week. The learning actually gets consolidated. Models don't have that loop. We've tried to approximate it with retrieval and long context, and those help, but they're really a kind of prosthetic. You're putting the experience in front of the model rather than letting it change the model.

The second thing, which I think is related, is that models mostly learn from a very narrow kind of feedback. In pretraining it's "predict the next token," and in post-training it's a reward signal that a human or a reward model produced. In the real world, the feedback is much richer and much messier. You take an action, something happens in the world three steps later, and you have to attribute that outcome back to the decision you made. Models are still pretty bad at that kind of long-horizon credit assignment, especially when the signal is sparse or ambiguous.

And then there's a practical problem that I think people underrate, which is that learning from experience at scale means learning from deployment. Millions of users, all interacting with the model in different ways. If you want the model to actually get better from that, you need to figure out what counts as a good outcome without just optimizing for whatever people click on, because that gets you something pretty unhealthy quickly. So the missing piece isn't only an algorithmic one. It's also about having the right environment and the right objective so that continual learning makes the model better rather than just more sycophantic.

Where I'm optimistic is that this is becoming the frontier now. The pretraining scaling story is still real, but the returns are getting more expensive, and the obvious next lever is letting models accumulate experience over time, in agentic settings, where they're actually doing things and seeing the consequences. I think the next couple of years are going to be much more about that than about just stacking more data.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that after deployment the model’s weights are static and that it cannot retain what it learns from interactions, identifying this as a barrier to learning from subsequent experience.

astra-6.text:
I think the big missing piece is that they don’t really learn continuously from interacting with the world. They can adapt within a conversation—you can correct them, give them new information, and they’ll use it—but that’s different from updating the model itself. You haven’t necessarily taught it something that it will carry into the next interaction.

What you’d like is a system that can try something, observe the outcome, and get better because of that experience. If it makes a mistake and you explain why, it should be able to retain that lesson and apply it in a different situation, rather than needing the same correction again.

The challenge is deciding what to learn from. An interaction might contain useful feedback, or it might contain something wrong. So it’s not just about giving models memory. It’s about letting them accumulate experience while being selective about what that experience teaches them.

r001.rationale: The response says models do not update themselves from interactions and may not carry lessons into later interactions, but it does not identify frozen weights after deployment as the barrier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big thing that’s missing is the ability to try something, see whether it worked, and change your behavior based on that outcome. These models learn an enormous amount during training, but once you deploy them, their parameters are typically frozen. They can adapt within a conversation, but that’s different from learning something that persists into the next interaction.

If you think about how we learn, a lot of it comes from acting in the world and getting feedback. You make a prediction, you make a mistake, and you update. We need a much better version of that loop for models: the ability to accumulate experience and improve from it, without forgetting what they already know or absorbing every bad piece of feedback they encounter.

r001.rationale: It says deployed models typically have frozen parameters, distinguishing that from persistent learning through later interactions.
